additions.title: Walking Shakyamuni Buddha
additions.rationale: Pairs two distinct ways to make walking legible. The complete Thai figure contrasts with Rodin’s deliberately incomplete body; it adds an Asian example to a strongly European sequence without adding another struggle or athlete.
additions.caption: The lowered gaze, lifted heel, and flowing robe turn a step into an image of calm teaching. Walking Buddhas are characteristic of Sukhothai sculpture in Thailand. Compare this complete figure with Rodin’s Walking Man: each makes a fixed body suggest a different kind of movement.

additions.title: Gold Dinar of al-Muktafi
additions.rationale: A deliberate change from ruler portraits to authority expressed through text, precious material and a portable object. Introduces Abbasid Baghdad at a radically different physical scale.
additions.caption: Authority is carried here by gold and writing. This dinar was struck at Madinat al-Salam, Baghdad, in 290 AH (902–903 CE), during the reign of al-Muktafi. Turn it to compare the inscriptions on both sides. The original coin is only 21 mm across; the separate bar belongs to the recording.

additions.title: Clava, Insignia of Authority
additions.rationale: Adds authority embodied in an actual hand-held insignia, alongside sculpted rulers and protective figures. The next Katsina stop keeps the comparison between distinct American contexts explicit rather than merging them.
additions.caption: The Chilean museum identifies this carved stone clava as an insignia of authority. Its broad head, narrow grip, incised lines, and pierced handle give status a form that could be held. Compare these choices with the costume and posture of the figures elsewhere in the exhibition.

additions.title: Abbasid Tombstone
additions.rationale: Introduces an Islamic commemorative object through its own inscribed form. Pairing two Egyptian funerary objects prompts comparison while preserving the differences between their dates, traditions and purposes.
additions.caption: Rows of Arabic writing cover this marble tombstone, dated 830 CE and recorded as Egyptian, probably from Fustat. Its inscribed field makes remembrance visible through words. Compare its layout with the false door, while keeping the different religious purposes and historical settings of the two works in mind.

additions.title: Shrine with Pietà
additions.rationale: A close subject comparison with Michelangelo, but a different scale, material and setting: a cottage façade shrine. It makes the theme of devotion concrete rather than merely adding another saint.
additions.caption: This painted wooden Pietà once hung on the front of a cottage in Chochołów, Poland. The carved figures and their shelter belong together. Compare it with Michelangelo’s Pietà: the shared subject takes a different form in a shrine made for the setting of a home.

additions.title: Venus of Lespugue
additions.rationale: Adds a precise, documented episode of damage during discovery, followed by copying for access. Extends the sequence beyond its concentration of Mediterranean heads and torsos without treating every incomplete form as accidental damage.
additions.caption: This mammoth-ivory figure was damaged by excavation tools when it was discovered in 1922. The digital model records a mold of the original. Look for the difference between the surviving outline and the damaged surfaces: discovery and later copying have both shaped how the sculpture is encountered.

additions.title: Iznik Jug with English Mounts
additions.rationale: Ends with survival through embellishment and reuse rather than another isolated fragment. Historic English mounts on an Ottoman jug make collection history visible in the joins and mixed materials.
additions.caption: This Ottoman fritware jug acquired silver-gilt mounts in London around 1592. The metal covers the rim, handle, and foot and adds a hinged lid. The Fitzwilliam explains that these additions protected fragile edges and made the vessel more luxurious. Look at the joins to follow its changing form.

additions.title: Long Rongorongo Tablet
additions.rationale: Contrasts carved narrative on curved ivory with rows of writing on curved wood. Adds Rapa Nui and a limit of interpretation: recording signs in3D does not decipher them.
additions.caption: Closely incised signs follow the curved wooden surface of this Rongorongo tablet from Rapa Nui. The museum records 1,580 glyphs and notes that the writing remains undeciphered. Rotate the tablet to follow the rows around it; seeing the cuts clearly is different from knowing what they say.

additions.title: Nasrid Casket
additions.rationale: A compact final stop joins carving, drilling, precious underlying material and later paint. Adds the Islamic West and makes surface a layered construction rather than decoration alone.
additions.caption: Carved and drilled ivory panels expose gold leaf beneath the casket’s stars and rosettes. Painting was added to the smooth areas in the fifteenth century. Move around the lid and sides to distinguish openings, shallow carving, and painted marks: several kinds of surface work coexist on this small box.

captionCorrections.before: This quartzite head from Tell el-Amarna represents a daughter of Akhenaten. The elongated skull follows the Amarna style; the missing body is the result of later loss rather than part of the design.
captionCorrections.after: This cast records an Amarna-period head identified as a queen, possibly Kiya or Meritaten. The museum leaves the sitter’s identity open. Compare the unfinished facial areas and short surviving neck; the cast preserves the small head, while its modern mount supplies a separate support.
captionCorrections.reason: The exact original is BerlinÄM21245, with unfinished facialareas and shortneck; the old daughter-of-Akhenaten identification and elongated-cranium description concern a different or overconfident interpretation.
